items.q: You can't fully understand every line of the code the AI wrote. Where should you focus your reading?
options: Every line equally, or don't review at all
The parts that touch your data, files, money, or secrets — and whether the shape and names match what you asked
Nothing — if it runs, it's fine

explain.right: Skim the plumbing, read closely the parts that can hurt you, and check the pieces and names match your intent.
explain.wrong: You don't need every line, comments aren't the truth, and 'it runs' alone doesn't mean it's safe or correct.

items.q: What are the three trust checks before relying on generated code?
options: Does it run, is it safe, does it do what the spec says
Did the AI sound confident, is it formatted nicely, is it recent
Is it long, is it clever, is it well-commented
Is it short, is it fast, is it popular

explain.right: Runs, safe, correct — execute it, scan for anything dangerous, then check it against your acceptance criteria.
explain.wrong: Length, cleverness, confidence, and formatting say nothing about whether code works or is safe.

items.q: The AI's code calls a function and running it errors with 'is not a function'. Most likely explanation?
options: You need to switch programming languages
That library is always wrong and should never be used
The model invented a plausible-but-nonexistent API — a hallucination to verify against the real docs

explain.right: Because it predicts plausible text, the model can confidently invent APIs; running the code is what exposes them.
explain.wrong: It's not your machine, the whole library, or your language at fault — it's a made-up call to check and replace.

options: Trust it more when it sounds confident
Give it the real documentation (or let it fetch the docs with a tool) and run the code

explain.right: Grounding it in real docs plus actually executing the code catches invented calls — confident tone doesn't.
explain.wrong: Forceful or longer prompts and trusting confidence don't add real facts; grounding and running do.

items.q: Name two things you check before trusting code the AI wrote, and why each matters.
rubric: Names at least two of: does it run, is it safe, does it match the spec
Explains that running catches errors/invented APIs
Explains that 'safe' guards against secrets/destructive actions, and 'matches spec' means it meets the acceptance criteria

explain.right: Strong answers pick two real checks (e.g. run it to catch invented APIs; verify it against the spec) with reasons.
explain.wrong: A weak answer lists vague traits like 'looks clean' without tying them to runs/safe/correct.
